items.title: Implant interview: Len Lemeire on ‘The Kinematics Of Doubt’
items.summary: Implant's Len Lemeire discusses 'The Kinematics Of Doubt,' out now on Alfa Matrix, doubt as a political tool, EBM and trance, and the 20 November show.
items.fullText:
Implant mainman Len Lemeire discusses ‘The Kinematics Of Doubt’, his fifteenth studio album as the long-running Belgian EBM project, in a new interview with Side-Line. The record came out on Alfa Matrix on October 30, 2026, in digital and CD editions, led by the single “Underneath The Neon Lights.”

Lemeire named the fourteen-track album after kinematics, the branch of physics that studies motion without asking what causes it, a frame he uses to talk about songwriting as a series of decisions: tempo, key, sound, arrangement, hook and lyrics all pushing a track somewhere else. In the interview, he talks about the title’s origins, the political uses of doubt, a guest vocal he recorded for Aiboforcen, the physics behind track titles such as “The Observer Effect” and “The Insider,” the EBM scene’s old suspicion of trance, and mastering work for other Alfa Matrix artists.

Implant shares a double release night with Llumen at mOtown in Sint-Joost-ten-Node on November 20, with interactive visuals by Pieter Coussement.

Implant interview

Side-Line: In physics, kinematics describes movement without asking what causes it. Why borrow that frame? Is it also a refusal to explain why you make the music you make?

Len: Kinematics is, quite literally, the study of motion. What attracted me to the term was the idea that composing is also a process of movement. Every decision pushes a track somewhere else: the BPM, the key, the sounds, the arrangement, the hook, the lyrics. At some point during the making of the album, I started to see this almost as a dance between doubt and decisions that worked. That is where “The Kinematics of Doubt” came from.

So I would not say the title is a refusal to explain why I make the music I make. If anything, the reason can probably be traced back to a kind of reverse childhood trauma.

My parents were actually very open-minded when it came to music. I could play almost anything at home without much reaction. But when I discovered Front 242, that was apparently the limit. I still remember my father standing at the bottom of the stairs shouting: “Turn that noise off!” And, well… the rest is history.

Side-Line: The album also has a track called “The Observer Effect”: in physics, measuring a system changes it. Kinematics, observation, are you writing a physics album about people?

Len: Haha, not really. Choosing an album title is always a long process for me. Once I have one, though, I do tend to start seeing connections around it and building on it as I go.

“The Observer Effect” is a good example. The track was originally called “The Hawthorne Effect,” after the psychological concept that people change their behaviour when they know they are being observed. A very simple example would be sitting at a red light with a police car next to you: even if you are doing absolutely nothing wrong, you suddenly become much more conscious of how you behave. The lyrics take that idea into relationships. Couples often develop a certain way of behaving when they are together, and I find it fascinating how different people can become when their partner, the “observer” in this case, is no longer there.

So no, I did not deliberately set out to make a physics album about people. But the record is very much about human interaction, and in hindsight that is actually quite an interesting thing to look at through the idea of movement as well: how people influence each other, change direction, adapt, react and pull one another into different patterns. I genuinely enjoy it when someone discovers layers like that in the music, even when they were not consciously designed that way. I always hope music can carry ideas as well as sound, so if it makes someone think beyond the immediate track, I take that as a compliment.

Side-Line: What were you certain about in 1996, when “Fun” came out, that you’ve since let go of? And what are you still unsure of today?

Len: When “Fun” came out, I was 26. I am 56 now, so inevitably the things you are certain about, and the things you are afraid of, change quite dramatically.

I recently did a guest vocal for Aiboforcen about the period when I first got to know Seba and Benoit. One of the lines goes: “We were young, a bit naive. We fought the demons in our minds.” I do not usually like explaining lyrics too much, but that line probably says something about the difference. Back then, we were singing about our fears and our demons, but we were also incredibly naive. At 26, a lot of your uncertainty is directed towards the future: what will happen, whether things will work out, whether you will become the person you think you are supposed to become. At 56, the uncertainty is different. In some ways, the fears become less selfish because you have children and there are people whose future matters to you at least as much as your own. They also become more concrete. You start seeing people around you disappear, slowly but inevitably, and time stops being an abstract concept.

So perhaps what I have let go of is the certainty that there will always be enough time to figure everything out. What am I still unsure of today? Probably most things that really matter. The difference is that I am much more comfortable with that than I was at 26.

Side-Line: Doubt has become a political tool: manufactured uncertainty about science, elections, facts. Does the album separate the doubt that frees you from the doubt that’s used against you?

Len: Doubt has definitely become a political tool. It can be a very effective way of creating division, although I would argue that doubt itself is often only the weapon, polarization is the broader strategy. A lot of political communication today is built around defining a problem in the strongest and clearest possible terms. But being very good at identifying a problem does not automatically mean you have a good solution for it. I think we sometimes confuse those two things. If someone describes a problem in a way that strongly resonates with us, we become more inclined to trust the solution they offer as well.

The problem is that a powerful diagnosis often benefits from simplification and extremes, whereas actually explaining something requires nuance. And nuance is much harder to communicate. There is a difference between naming a problem effectively and genuinely explaining it. But that is quite different from the doubt on “The Kinematics of Doubt.” The album is much more concerned with doubt as part of movement and creation: questioning a decision, changing direction, trying something else and eventually arriving somewhere.

For me, that is almost the opposite of manufactured doubt. Productive doubt opens possibilities. Doubt that is deliberately used against you usually tries to restrict them. At that point, it stops being curiosity and starts becoming manipulation.

Side-Line: “Information Systems” is built entirely from spoken samples about the mythology of computing. Which myths did you want to expose and why open with voices instead of a beat?

Len: “Information Systems” basically functions as the introduction to the EP. I wanted it to open with something that was not immediately a beat-driven track, but that created a context before the music really started moving.

The subject also comes quite naturally to me. In everyday life I am a university professor, and one of the subjects I teach to first-year economics students deals with the role of information systems in organisations. But I am at least as fascinated by the role computers have acquired in our everyday lives. We hardly notice most of these systems anymore, precisely because they have become so deeply embedded in how we live.

That fascination has become even stronger with the current discussion around AI and ideas such as “human in the loop.” There seems to be a growing tendency to regard computer involvement itself as problematic in certain areas, particularly when we talk about creativity and art. I understand where that discussion comes from, but I also find the contradiction interesting. We may strongly object to an algorithm interfering with art, while being perfectly happy to let another algorithm tell us where we can buy something for the lowest price.

What interests me is that underneath all those different applications, the basic principle remains remarkably simple. Computers perform computations. AI may appear mysterious, intelligent or even threatening, and an online recommendation system may appear completely mundane, but both ultimately emerge from enormous sequences of calculations.

That is why one of the samples in the track, “computations are carried out,” is almost the key line for me. There is a mythology surrounding computers because we tend to focus on what their output appears to mean rather than on what the machine is actually doing.

And that is also why I wanted to start with voices rather than a beat. It works almost like a small lecture or statement of intent before the EP begins. The rhythm comes afterwards; first I wanted the idea to enter the room.

Side-Line: “The Insider” asks how much of what we call fact is really interpretation. Who’s the insider in 2026: the expert, the algorithm, or the person who leaks?

Len: “The Insider” is really about the one-eyed man in the land of the blind. I don’t think anybody truly has “inside information” unless they are actually involved in shaping the thing itself. Experts are not necessarily insiders. They may understand the structure extremely well, but that is still different from being at the origin of it. An algorithm is something else again. Most of the time, it is a mechanism for supporting or automating decisions: who gets shown which music, what the next word in a sentence should be, which information reaches which person. It does not really “know” in the human sense; it classifies, ranks and predicts. And the person who leaks information is different again. That is often somebody who was close enough to help shape something, but who may no longer agree with the shape it has taken.

If you connect those three to doubt, you actually get three completely different forms of it. The expert doubts the nature or interpretation of the structure. The algorithm replaces doubt with classification and probability. The leaker may doubt whether something should remain hidden in the first place.

But the song itself is less about those three categories and more about the person who knows one fragment of the picture and then starts behaving as if they understand the entire artefact. That is the kind of “insider” I was interested in: someone who possesses a piece of the truth and mistakes that piece for the whole.

Side-Line: The record circles control, obsession, surveillance, manipulation, identity and truth. EBM grew up on images of uniforms and factories. Is today’s control more intimate than a boot on the street?

Len: The record is indeed very much about human interaction, and I think observing human interaction only becomes really interesting when you start looking at the boundaries. Almost every subject you mention, control, obsession, surveillance, manipulation, identity, truth, exists somewhere on a borderline. And human behaviour has a tendency to test those borders, to see what happens on the other side.

For me, EBM has always done something similar. It is a genre that probes boundaries. And the most interesting modern forms of EBM are crossing boundaries with other musical styles. I think that is also part of its origins, although the imagery traditionally associated with EBM, uniforms, factories, discipline, machinery, has not always been entirely consistent with what the songs were actually about. When I hear Nitzer Ebb sing “if you smile you can’t take it back,” for instance, I also hear an observation about human behaviour rather than simply an industrial aesthetic.

Control itself has also become much more complex. We have found ways of scaling up very personal forms of control through social media, algorithms and visibility. What used to happen between individuals can now be amplified to thousands or millions of people. Jimmy Carr, one of my favourite stand-up comedians, once made the joke that socialism is the redistribution of wealth, while social media is the redistribution of status. There is quite a lot of truth in that. Status, attention and visibility have become things that can be measured, distributed and manipulated.

So yes, I think control today is often much more intimate than a boot on the street. It can sit inside the way we present ourselves, the way we compare ourselves to others, the information we receive and even the way we start adjusting our behaviour.

Side-Line: “Transaction Failure,” “Beyond The Code,” “On TV”: money, software, media. Are those the three machines that manufacture doubt today?

Len: They are certainly machines that can produce doubt, but they are not the only ones. Doubt itself is not necessarily something negative. In many ways, it is fundamental to both science and religion. The most intelligent people I know usually leave some room for uncertainty in what they know, not because they distrust their own knowledge, but because they understand that very few things come with complete answers.

That is where it becomes interesting. The moment someone claims to have the complete solution, I become suspicious. Very often, certainty is also a form of power. If you can replace doubt with belief in one clear answer, one system or one explanation, you will always find people willing to follow that story. That is also why science can be frustrating. Science spends enormous amounts of time trying to reduce uncertainty, test assumptions and eliminate alternative explanations. Creating doubt is much easier than producing certainty.

So yes, money, software and media can all manufacture doubt, but the more important mechanism is perhaps the promise that doubt can be removed completely. That promise is often much more powerful than doubt itself.

Side-Line: Trance is back in the mix. Around 2000 the industrial scene looked down on it. Did the scene owe trance an apology looking backward?

Len: There are definitely a few trance ideas on the album, even some Goa influences, but also techno and melodic techno. I have never been very interested in treating genres as fixed territories. Those categories can be useful to describe music, but they become limiting very quickly if you start treating them as rules.

So does the industrial scene owe trance an apology? Maybe a little. Around 2000 there was certainly a tendency to look down on certain styles simply because they belonged to another scene or carried a different aesthetic. Looking back, that seems rather pointless to me. If an idea works, it works. All those boxes are there to be broken down anyway.

Side-Line: You master a lot of Alfa Matrix releases. Does hearing everyone else’s work up close make you more doubtful of your own or more confident?

Len: Mastering is quite a technical discipline, and I really see it as something different from writing or producing music. I always consider it a great honour when somebody trusts me with the final sound of an album or EP, because that is an important stage in shaping the end product. My job is to make the music come across as well as possible without imposing myself on it.

Compilations are slightly different. There you are often dealing with an overview of a period, a scene or a label, so consistency becomes very important. With an album or an EP, it feels much more personal because you are dealing with one artist’s complete vision.

Of course, listening to so much music that closely does affect the way I hear things. Sometimes I hear something and think, “Damn, I wish I had done that,” or “I should have tried that in a mix.” And sometimes I hear something and think that maybe there was more that could have been brought out of it. But to be honest, I have that with music all the time, even when I am simply listening in the car. Once you make music yourself, you never really listen in a completely passive way anymore. Whether you want to or not, part of your brain is always imagining the tracks in the DAW, wondering how something was built, mixed or arranged. So I would not say it makes me more doubtful or more confident. Both I guess.

Side-Line: You’ve worked with Front 242, Anne Clark and Noemi Aurora. What did a collaborator ever teach you that you couldn’t have taught yourself?

Len: Every collaboration has been unique, and I genuinely think I learned something from every single one of them. The list is actually much longer than those three, and every person on that list brought something different. Sometimes it was musical, sometimes technical, sometimes simply a different way of approaching an idea or making a decision.

What I probably value most, though, is the fact that music has allowed me to meet so many interesting people. Most of those connections started from a very simple place: mutual respect for each other’s music. I feel genuinely blessed that music has given me the opportunity to work with all those people and to build those connections along the way.

Side-Line: On November 20 you share a release night with Llumen at mOtown. Pieter Coussement also does Implant’s visuals. Does the image follow the sound, or does it sometimes lead?

Len: Pieter has programmed quite a lot for the visual side of the Implant live show. Some elements are prepared video clips, but there is always an interactive layer on top that he controls live. The visuals react to what happens on stage. Even when I play certain sounds on the keyboard, that can trigger an effect or a visual response and a sound. So the image is quite interactive rather than simply running alongside the music. Pieter also handles a few sound effects and additional elements during the show. All in all, it is definitely more than just pressing play on a laptop. The tracks themselves have also been reworked into proper live versions, so both the sound and the visuals are adapted for the stage.

On November 20, I would describe the show at mOtown almost as a preview or a try-out for that setup. Llumen also has a very strong new album out, so it felt like the perfect opportunity to combine both releases in one evening. And because Pieter is involved in both projects, there is a natural connection between them. We are hoping that the Llumen-Implant combination is something we can bring to a few more stages after that as well.

So does the image follow the sound? Sometimes, yes. But because so much of it is interactive, there are also moments where sound and image are really influencing each other rather than one simply following the other.

About Implant

Implant is the electro-industrial project Len Lemeire started in Belgium in 1996. That year’s debut CD single, “Fun,” credited Lemeire alongside Geert Machtelinck and was pressed in a numbered edition of 1,000 copies. Built on EBM sequencing, physical electronics and a recurring catchphrase, “did you have your Implant today?,” the project went on to release albums including “Implantology,” “Audio Blender,” “The Productive Citizen” and “Soft Flesh – Hard Steel,” alongside the EP “Fading Away.”

Lemeire released the free download single “The Drive” in December 2023, followed by the twelfth studio album, “The Chaos Machines Part 1 – No More Flies On The Windscreen,” in May 2024. The trilogy continued with the limited vinyl EP “The Chaos Machines Part 2 – Scratching The Surface” in September 2024 and closed with “Judging Sinners – The Chaos Machines Part 3” on February 7, 2025, a ten-track album again featuring Noemi Aurora. Lemeire has also recorded with Front 242 and Anne Clark, and mastered releases across the Alfa Matrix roster.

“The Kinematics Of Doubt,” Implant’s fifteenth studio album, followed on October 30, 2026, on Alfa Matrix, in digital and CD. Lemeire marks the record with a double release night alongside Llumen at mOtown in Sint-Joost-ten-Node on November 20, with interactive visuals by longtime collaborator Pieter Coussement.

items.title: La Chanson Noire’s ‘Grand Mal’ single out now via Violeta Exotica
items.summary: La Chanson Noire's single "Grand Mal," produced by Charles Sangnoir at Studio Vitruve in Paris, is out now digitally through Violeta Exotica.
items.fullText:
Goth and darkwave project La Chanson Noire’s single “Grand Mal” is out now digitally through Violeta Exotica, following the track’s official video, which the project released on 1 October.

Charles Sangnoir produced “Grand Mal” at Studio Vitruve in Paris. The video was filmed in Paris with contributions from Vanda Spengler and Emile Gontard, on screen and behind the camera. “Grand Mal” is La Chanson Noire’s first single since 2024’s “Missa Negra.”

La Chanson Noire plays two shows around the release: 31 October in Paris at Noisy Pop Club, and 19 December in Corroios, Portugal, at Cine Teatro G.C. with Trash Circus.

About La Chanson Noire

Charles Sangnoir started La Chanson Noire in 2007, blending cabaret, punk, post-punk, rock and opera into a theatrical sound. The project’s debut EP, “Canções De Faca E Alguidar,” came out that year through Necrosymphonic Entertainment, followed by a split release with Espelho Mau, “Gay Music For Straight People,” on the same label in 2008. The 7″ single “O Bordel De Lúcifer,” a limited black-vinyl pressing shared across Raging Planet, HelloOutro Enterprises and Chaosphere Recordings, arrived in 2009.

The project’s debut album, “Música Para Os Mortos,” arrived in 2010 as a limited CD. “Cabaret Portugal” followed in 2012, “Macumba Stereo” in 2013 and “Evergloom,” issued in a limited special edition, in 2016, each released through the same Raging Planet, Chaosphere Recordings, Raising Legends Records and Necrosymphonic Entertainment network. “Cruz Credo,” released in 2020, marked La Chanson Noire’s first work with Violeta Exotica, the label that also issued 2024’s “Missa Negra” alongside Larvae Records, Chaosphere Recordings and Raging Planet.

Current members are Sangnoir and Pedro Almeida, joined on record and on stage by rotating guest musicians. “Grand Mal” continues the project’s run with Violeta Exotica, now the label behind its last three releases.

items.title: Foule release new single ‘Aurore’
items.summary: French dark wave duo Foule release the single "Aurore" on October 31, 2026, following their 2026 debut album "Porcelaine".
items.fullText:
French dark wave duo Foule have released the single “Aurore” on October 31, 2026, their first new material since the 2026 debut album “Porcelaine”.

The track is credited to Zoe Boutin on vocals and lyrics and Olly on guitar and machines, the same duo behind “Porcelaine”. Side-Line’s review of that album described Foule’s sound as a blend of dark wave, post-punk and elements the duo themselves call “dark trap,” “industrial” and “witch house.”

According to the band, “Aurore” marks a shift in direction: still dark, but more minimalist, and less wounded than earlier material. Where “Porcelaine” leaned into tragedy, Foule describe “Aurore” as turning toward transformation, with the narrative moving away from pain and toward the possibility of hope.

“Porcelaine,” released in February 2026, collected ten tracks built around the tension between tenderness and violence, a theme the band linked to the Japanese art of kintsugi, which repairs broken porcelain with gold rather than hiding the damage.

About Foule

Foule is a French duo formed in 2023 by Zoe Boutin, who handles vocals and lyrics, and Olly, who plays guitar and machines. The band released a series of singles after forming, most of which were later collected on their debut album, “Porcelaine,” in February 2026.

Side-Line reviewed “Porcelaine” on its release, rating the album 8.5 out of 10 and highlighting its blend of dark wave, post-punk and industrial elements alongside the duo’s poetic, French-language lyrics. Side-Line also interviewed Foule around the album’s release, where the band described their music as “electronic and organic, dark but playful, delicate yet violent, raw yet poetic.”

With “Aurore,” Foule continue past “Porcelaine” with a single the band describes as more minimalist and more resilient than their earlier work.

items.title: Pyogenesis release video for ‘Sing As If’ ahead of ‘Adolescence’
items.summary: Pyogenesis release the official video for "Sing As If," the fourth single from their album "Adolescence," due January 15, 2027 on Massacre Records.
items.fullText:
German gothic and alternative metal band Pyogenesis have released the official video for “Sing As If”, the fourth single from their upcoming album “Adolescence,” due January 15, 2027 on Massacre Records.

Frontman Flo V. Schwarz is joined on the track by his daughter Johanna, who contributes vocals. According to Schwarz, “Sing As If” looks back at youth and first love, and the moments spent working out the difference between loving someone and simply being in love. Schwarz also stated that the video was shot at the same location used for Ridley Scott’s “Blade Runner.”

“Adolescence” will be Pyogenesis’ first full-length album since 2020’s “A Silent Soul Screams Loud.” Side-Line reported in October that the record is coming via Massacre Records, with three CD release shows set for January 2027. “Sing As If” is the fourth single released from the album, following “All I Am Is Bleeding,” recorded with horror-punk band The Other, “Uncontrolled” and “Nothing But My Heart,” which the band has described as its first power-metal song in 35 years.

Pyogenesis will play three consecutive CD release shows in January 2027:

  • January 14 – Hamburg, Markthalle / Marx
  • January 15 – Bochum, Matrix / Rockpalast
  • January 16 – Munich, Backstage

Tickets and further information are available through pyogenesis.hamburgrecords.com.

About Pyogenesis

Pyogenesis formed in Stuttgart, Germany, in 1991, growing out of the local band Immortal Hate around singer and guitarist Flo V. Schwarz. The band’s first releases, the 1991 demo “Ode to the Churning Seas of Nar-Mataru” and the 1992 EP “Ignis Creatio” on Osmose Productions/SPV, placed the band in the death and doom metal scene of the time.

Through the mid and late 1990s, Pyogenesis released music tied to the emerging German gothic metal movement before moving toward alternative rock and pop-punk on 1997’s “Unpop,” released on Nuclear Blast/Warner Music. “Mono… or Will It Ever Be the Way It Used to Be” followed in 1998, and “She Makes Me Wish I Had a Gun” came out on Hamburg Records/Sony Music in 2002. The same years produced the EPs “Waves of Erotasia” in 1994, “Love Nation Sugarhead” in 1996 and “I Feel Sexy” in 2002.

The band went quiet for over a decade before returning in 2014 with a line-up change that brought in guitarist Gizz Butt, previously of The Prodigy. The heavier comeback era produced a trilogy of albums for AFM Records: “A Century in the Curse of Time” in 2015, “A Kingdom to Disappear” in 2017 and “A Silent Soul Screams Loud” in 2020, the last of which reached No. 33 on the German album charts.

The current line-up, with Flo V. Schwarz on vocals and guitar, Gizz Butt on guitar, Malte Brauer on bass and Sebastian Michalski on drums, signed to Massacre Records for “Adolescence.” The album follows the 2026 EP “Nothing but My Heart” and arrives with three CD release shows in Hamburg, Bochum and Munich in January 2027.

items.title: Camilla Pisani – Konstellationen (Digital/CD Album – Aesthetical)
items.summary: Camilla Pisani is an Italian audiovisual artist who has already released several albums and now...
items.fullText:
Camilla Pisani is an Italian audiovisual artist who has already released several albums and now returns with “Konstellationen”, her second album released via Aesthetical, a sub-label of Cyclic Law. At the heart of her artistic practice lies rhythm—the fundamental principle connecting music, astronomy, and human perception, transforming diverse forms of expression into a unified creative language.

“Konstellationen” comprises six tracks in which an astral atmosphere remains prominent, interwoven with slow-paced rhythms. The mostly extended compositions unfold gradually, occasionally incorporating Experimental elements such as field recordings. Ranging from Minimal-Electro to Experimental-Techno, this album has a great deal to offer. It is a varied work, yet one held together by a clear artistic vision that gives the entire album a strong sense of cohesion.

“Konstellationen” feels as though it were crafted in a sonic laboratory—a remark I intend as a high compliment, as we are dealing with an artist who genuinely understands the essence of creativity. (Rating:8).

Listen to “A Sob Against Sadness”:

About Camilla Pisani

Camilla Pisani is an audiovisual artist based in Rome, Italy, working in dark ambient, soundscape, noise and minimal electronic music. Her work combines field recordings, suspended atmospheres and concrete rhythms, built around the interaction between space, sound and abstract graphic signs.

Pisani’s discography includes the albums “Verneshot” (Ovunqve, 2017) and “Inner Spaces Like Anechoic Chambers” (MU Versatile Label, 2019), the collaborative album “Lithium Salt” with Banished Pills (2018), the self-released EP “Nausea Is A Noble Feeling” (2020) and “Frozen Archimia” (Midira Records, 2020).

She released her first album for Cyclic Law sub-label Aesthetical, “Phant[as]”, in 2022, followed by “Konstellationen” in 2026.

About Author & Punisher

Author & Punisher released its debut album, “The Painted Army,” in 2005. “Warcry” (2007) and “Drone Machines” (2010) came next, then “Ursus Americanus” (2012) and “Women & Children” (2013) on Seventh Rule Recordings. Shone moved to Phil Anselmo’s Housecore Records for “Melk en Honing” (2015) and “Pressure Mine” (2017), then signed to Relapse Records for “Beastland” (2018), “Kruller” (2022), which added guest musicians to the project for the first time, and “Nocturnal Birding” (2025). Shone self-released the live album “Live B.C. 2020” in 2020. After “Kruller,” guitarist Doug Sabolick joined Shone for live dates, the first time Author & Punisher performed on stage with another musician. items.title: “I Hear The Dead Calling My Name” — Sacramento Deathrock Outfit In Retrograde Descend into Darkness With “Cold Read”
items.summary: I’m losing my mind I can feel my soul being lost, trapped, stranded in time Deep voices travel strangely through old houses. They pass beneath doors, collect in stairwells, and… The post “I Hear The Dead Calling My Name” — Sacramento Deathrock Outfit In Retrog
items.fullText:
I’m losing my mind
I can feel my soul being lost, trapped, stranded in time

Deep voices travel strangely through old houses. They pass beneath doors, collect in stairwells, and make an invitation from the drawing room sound like an excellent reason to leave. Sacramento’s In Retrograde furnish those rooms with choral textures, droning guitars, and rhythms that suggest somebody downstairs has started running. Their deathrock has a taste for aristocratic excess, with enough physical force to send the furniture skidding.

Based in Sacramento, California, and active since 2018, the BIPOC deathrock and post-punk band draws from gothic rock’s theatrical vocabulary and the severity of black metal. Their five-track Cold Read demo brings their current sound into focus through new material and fresh mixes of earlier songs. The demo arrived on Bandcamp on October 12, 2026, with a wider streaming release announced for Halloween. It also offers a route back to The Lovers, the 2023 two-track release containing crowd favorite Two Lovers.

Shattered Sun (2026 mix) opens the ballroom doors with a firm drumbeat, choral atmosphere, and a deathrock guitar drone. Baroque flourishes accumulate in the dense arrangement, while the voice descends toward Peter Steele’s deepest register before climbing into the emotional agitation of the Birthday Party’s Release the Bats and Mr. Clarinet, with something of Tuxedomoon’s No Tears in its heightened delivery. The song’s original published lyrics describe faith and identity disintegrating under divine abandonment, with eternal life becoming a sentence of repeated suffering. That grand vocal presence belongs to someone whose impressive residence has become a prison.

Boots seem to hit the ground running on Man Love. Rapid drums, ominous guitar tones, and bass that penetrates to the bone suggest a lantern-lit carriage racing through the night with demons in pursuit. The singer moves between a deep lower register and high notes, pressing against the packed arrangement. Its lyrics bring explicit desire into contact with crucifixion imagery, turning pleasure, authority, and punishment into an ugly struggle. Heard alongside that relentless rhythm, the encounter has a coercive menace that makes the imagined chase feel especially urgent.

Despite its title, Italian Disco (2026 mix) is far removed from Italo disco. A low guitar drone recalls Bauhaus’s Dark Entries, while string-like tones rise through the mix and the drums maintain a shuffling gait. The subterranean vocals approach Peter Steele’s cavernous delivery, lending the song the atmosphere of Dante’s descent into hell. The lyrics tie that sense of damnation to lost love: the singer recalls a summer separation, imagines an invitation to dance, and faces the prospect of eternity without the person they desire.

Effects give the opening strums of Italian Disco II a dark electrical buzz. Cymbals sizzle, drums boom, and atmospheric layers build around a steady forward rhythm. A low vocal growl moves through sustained drones and resonant, bowed-string-like tones, lending the proceedings an elegant romance. The arrangement keeps adding weight around the voice, with each new layer making the space feel more sumptuous and enclosed.

The demo closes with the title track Cold Read, which begins with ominous strumming and broad atmospheric textures. Its shuffling drums gather momentum over deep, propulsive bass, while the vocal smolders in a whispered growl. A rising and falling melodic figure leaves space between sustained stabs, giving the windswept mix a distinct shape. The lyrics return to the opener’s troubled relationship with time: the dead call, the mind threatens to give way, and the singer pleads for rescue from an existence experienced as confinement. Those separated notes sound like signals sent from somewhere difficult to reach.

Listen to the Cold Read demo below and order it here.

Released in April 2023, The Lovers offers an earlier glimpse of that appetite for romance and decay. Two Lovers begins with a high cello sound swaying through an atmosphere of gothic deterioration. A sudden yelp announces the band’s entrance into a much denser passage of bass and thick drumbeats. Here, the voice leans further toward Nick Cave’s Birthday Party performances, carrying a feverish Batcave abandon through the arrangement. The cello remains audible as the pressure increases, its melodic movement preserving the song’s elegance amid the commotion. The band’s description of it as a crowd favourite makes immediate sense.

Death Ablaze (2023 Mix) follows with hi-hat splashes and a deep bass groove that establish its rhythmic pull immediately. A wiry, melodic gothic rock guitar figure enters, followed by a voice pitched low enough to churn the marrow. The interplay between that guitar line and the vocal gives the song its particular pleasure: the melody holds its shape around the singer’s weight, each sharpening the effect of the other. It closes the pair with a concentrated dose of gothic rock’s physical appeal.

Listen to The Lovers below and order it here.

For a wider introduction, Transylvanian Recordings’ self-titled 2024 compilation gathers nine tracks from the band’s catalogue. Fans of Bauhaus, the Birthday Party, Tuxedomoon, and Type O Negative should find several inviting doors into this particular house.

items.title: “Killing Karma” — Milwaukee Post-Punk Outfit Seances Share Video for Assemblage 23’s Remix of Debut Single “Fade”
items.summary: I can’t tell what’s in your heart tonight Bathing in the moonlight I am tethered to this shoreline It will never be the same A label compilation, a Discman, and… The post “Killing Karma” — Milwaukee Post-Punk Outfit Seances Share Video for Assemblage 23’s Remi
items.fullText:
I can’t tell what’s in your heart tonight
Bathing in the moonlight
I am tethered to this shoreline
It will never be the same

A label compilation, a Discman, and a dwindling supply of batteries could constitute an entire musical education. Metropolis, Wax Trax!, and Cleopatra introduced listeners to songs that made anxiety move with purpose, sending them back to the liner notes for their next discovery. For Milwaukee, Wisconsin’s Seances, those compilations were formative listening. A new collaboration brings one of those early connections into the present.

Assemblage 23 has remixed Fade, Seances’ first single, giving its post-punk unease a charge of electronic euphoria. The accompanying video, premiering here, comes from filmmaker Kyle Arpke, who sends the song through a succession of saturated colours and disorienting optical effects.

On Assemblage 23’s remix of Fade, Seances’ Eric Arsnow explains:

“Being able to work with Assemblage 23 on this remix of Fade was a dream come true. I burned through so many batteries on my Discman with their music as a soundtrack to my teenage life.”

Sighing synth pads open the track, giving way to buzzing electronics and Eric Arsnow’s urgent baritone. His delivery carries the cornered intensity of Ian Curtis, each phrase pressing against the steady insistence of the rhythm. Around 45 seconds in, the higher synth figure takes flight, lifting the song into a rush of feeling while the beat maintains its stern course.

Assemblage 23’s Tom Shear leaves room for Jason Kartz’s guitar to cut across the electronics, its clipped offbeats bringing a trace of ska and reggae to the arrangement. Just shy of the two-minute mark, a fluid solo breaks through, its expressive turns setting the surrounding machinery into sharper relief. Think Joy Division’s existential strain meeting DAF’s physical insistence, with a melody capable of changing the temperature of the room.

The words keep returning to a shoreline, a place where time seems to split and familiar feelings become difficult to trust. Arsnow sets private uncertainty against an indifferent world, worn down by recurring drama and the sense of living through the same trouble again. When he sings, “I’m counting on us now,” the line feels like a hand extended through the confusion. The remix catches the existential beauty of that appeal, allowing dread and exhilaration to occupy the same measure.

Arpke translates that unstable perspective into overlapping bands of red, blue, purple, and green. Close-ups of Arsnow in sunglasses stretch and double around the microphone; silhouettes separate into coloured outlines, while an open book of hand-drawn symbols lends the footage an occult charge. Circular distortions make his face seem caught inside a turning lens, repeatedly brought into focus and pulled apart. It suits a song preoccupied with recognition and repetition, with a familiar figure becoming increasingly difficult to pin down.

Watch the video for the Assemblage 23 remix of Fade below:

Seances began taking shape after Arsnow saw The Chameleons in Milwaukee in 2023. Already steeped in The Cure and Joy Division, and encouraged by discoveries made while working in a record shop, the singer and bassist went home and outlined an album’s worth of songs through voice memos recorded on bass. Kartz helped develop Fade from those initial sketches, laying the foundations for the debut album Power Is A Phantom.

For the live incarnation of Seances, Arsnow recruited musicians associated with The Promise Ring, Masked Intruder, Tigernite, Fight Dice, and BvsMV. The band is now working on its second album, Silent Salvation, planned for 2027.

Listen to the Assemblage 23 remix of Fade below and order it here

Seances also recently released Tame, a tribute to Eric Arsnow’s late friend Francisco Ramirez, a musician, printmaker, and father. Written and performed by Arsnow and released on October 23, 2026, the song addresses the difficult business of continuing through life after losing someone, holding affection, anger, and the desire to feel joy again within the same embrace. Its artwork incorporates a photographic abstraction of Ramirez’s Florid Print, giving his own work a place within the tribute.

Available as a name-your-price download, the release also offers a way to support his family: Arsnow encourages listeners to contribute directly to the fundraiser for Ramirez’s daughter, and says any payments received through Bandcamp will be passed along to that fund as well.

items.title: Golden Apes headlines Halloween 30th-anniversary show at Wrocław’s Liverpool club
items.summary: Golden Apes headlined Shadows Veil and Her Own World at a Halloween show marking 30 years of Wrocław club Liverpool, October 31, 2026.
items.fullText:
Shadows Veil, Her Own World and Golden Apes, Liverpool club, Wrocław, Poland, October 31, 2026

There could hardly have been a more appropriate evening to celebrate thirty years of Liverpool than Halloween, with its peculiar affection for darkness, theatricality and everything that refuses to conform to the ordinary. The night of Samhain, poised between October and November, has always carried an atmosphere of transition, a moment when the familiar world seems to acquire another dimension. In a club whose history is so intimately connected with gothic, industrial and alternative music, that symbolism felt especially fitting.

Liverpool has witnessed three decades of musical transformations, generations of audiences, countless performances and the development of relationships that extend well beyond the walls of the venue. For its anniversary, Castle Party in the Club brought together three bands representing different shades of the darker musical spectrum: Shadows Veil, Her Own World and Golden Apes. Their respective approaches to gothic expression offered an evening of considerable musical variety, beautifully complemented by the atmosphere of the club, its evocative lighting and the unmistakable pleasure of celebrating Halloween in a place with such a remarkable history.

My relationship with Liverpool goes back many years, and the club itself, the people who have built its identity and the wonderful conversations I had throughout the evening deserve a separate story. For now, I want to concentrate on the performances, because the musicians provided a celebration worthy of the occasion.

Shadows Veil

Shadows Veil opened the evening, marking my first encounter with the project. There is something particularly enjoyable about discovering a band in a live setting, without the familiarity that inevitably accompanies artists one has followed for years. It allows the music to establish its own relationship with the listener, free from expectations accumulated through previous recordings and performances.

The band’s musical vocabulary draws upon post-punk, gothic rock and darkwave, with a pronounced appreciation for melancholic melodies and the rhythmic structures that have long characterized these traditions. Yet what I enjoyed most was the energy with which they approached their material. Their compositions possess a sense of forward movement that gives their darker melodic elements a more immediate physical presence.

The guitars contribute atmospheric depth without obscuring the rhythmic foundations, and the relationship between the instrumental arrangements and the melodies creates an appealing contrast between introspection and momentum. The music has a romantic quality, although its melancholy is accompanied by sufficient energy to prevent it from becoming excessively contemplative.

As the opening act, Shadows Veil provided an effective introduction to the evening, establishing a gothic atmosphere without exhausting its possibilities. Their performance felt particularly appropriate for a Halloween celebration, although its appeal extended well beyond the seasonal associations of the occasion.

I genuinely enjoyed their stage energy, their musical character and the opportunity to become acquainted with another interesting project. Their appearance encouraged me to explore their recordings more closely, and I consider that a particularly satisfying outcome of a first live encounter.

Her Own World

Her Own World followed with a performance that combined musical intensity, theatrical sophistication and a wonderfully considered visual presentation. Having followed the Szczecin-based band’s development for some time, I have become increasingly appreciative of their ability to integrate electronics, guitars, expressive vocals and visual storytelling into a coherent artistic identity.

For this particular occasion, the band presented beautiful new costumes, with striking red dresses that corresponded perfectly with the Halloween atmosphere. Against the darkness of the stage and the beautifully arranged lighting at Liverpool, the red acquired an almost dramatic intensity. It introduced an element of gothic elegance to a performance whose musical foundations remain considerably more forceful.

The visual effect was particularly successful because it belonged naturally to the band’s aesthetic. The costumes were neither an unrelated Halloween decoration nor an attempt to compensate for the music. They extended its emotional and theatrical dimensions. The relationship between the red dresses, the stage lighting and the darker electronic arrangements created an appealing interplay of beauty, danger and expressive intensity.

Her Own World’s music derives much of its character from the interaction between electronic precision and the more organic qualities of gothic and industrial rock. The programmed rhythms establish a powerful foundation, while the guitars introduce weight, texture and an additional degree of physicality. Rather than competing for dominance, these elements create a layered sound in which electronic discipline and instrumental force reinforce one another.

Yu’s vocals remain central to this arrangement. Her delivery carries considerable emotional expression, moving comfortably within music that can be both melodically accessible and intensely rhythmic. The contrast is especially effective in concert, where the voice introduces a distinctly human dimension to the controlled force of the electronic structures. Her stage presence, meanwhile, adds theatricality without reducing the performance to an exercise in visual spectacle.

What I increasingly appreciate about Her Own World is the care invested in the relationship between sound and image. Their visual language has become more assured, while the musical arrangements have developed greater confidence in balancing melody, rhythmic force and dramatic expression. The costumes and lighting at Liverpool illustrated that progression particularly beautifully.

There was also something rather delightful about seeing the band’s aesthetic interpreted through the visual possibilities of Halloween. The red dresses introduced a sense of ceremony and gothic extravagance, while the lighting gave the performance depth and atmosphere. It was stylish, visually memorable and musically satisfying, with sufficient energy to make the performance feel celebratory without compromising the darker character of the compositions.

Her Own World continue to develop as a live act, and watching that process remains a genuine pleasure. Their performance at Liverpool demonstrated how successfully they can combine theatrical elegance with the force and immediacy of contemporary dark electronic rock.

Golden Apes

The evening culminated with Golden Apes, whose music inhabits an entirely different emotional landscape, and one to which I have returned with affection for many years. As the headliners of Liverpool’s thirtieth-anniversary celebration, they brought a particular kind of elegance to the stage, rooted in the subtle relationship between musical restraint, expressive depth and emotional intensity.

Golden Apes have always possessed an exceptional ability to create atmosphere without allowing it to become an end in itself. Their compositions develop through beautifully measured instrumental arrangements, with the bass providing a dark, rounded weight, the guitars unfolding in layers of texture and melody, and the percussion giving the music its sense of movement.

Their sound has something almost tactile about it. It reminds me of velvet: substantial, absorbing, occasionally rough beneath the surface, yet capable of extraordinary softness. In concert, that quality becomes especially apparent, as the interplay of instruments allows the compositions to acquire a physical presence that recordings can only partially communicate.

Peer Lebrecht’s voice remains one of the band’s greatest treasures. Deep, resonant and unmistakably expressive, it possesses a rare capacity for communicating emotional complexity without resorting to exaggeration. His stage presence follows a similarly restrained aesthetic. There is a quiet authority to his delivery, an intimacy that draws the audience towards the music rather than demanding an immediate reaction.

Perhaps the most moving quality of Golden Apes, however, is the extraordinary relationship between strength and fragility that runs through their compositions. Their music can acquire an almost monumental presence through the weight of the bass, the density of the guitars and the measured insistence of the percussion, yet somewhere within that imposing architecture remains something profoundly vulnerable.

A melodic phrase may reveal an unexpected tenderness; a moment of vocal restraint may communicate considerably more than an emphatic declaration ever could. There is a beautiful emotional permeability to their music, as though its carefully constructed exterior were never intended to conceal the sensitivity underneath.

That contrast became particularly meaningful in the live setting. The physical strength of the instrumental arrangements existed alongside a remarkable delicacy of expression, allowing passages of considerable intensity to retain their emotional openness. The music could be commanding without becoming impenetrable, melancholic without surrendering to sentimentality, and deeply vulnerable without losing its dignity.

Golden Apes have cultivated this balance over decades, and it remains one of the reasons their work continues to resonate with me. Their compositions acknowledge the fragility of human experience while preserving an unmistakable sense of endurance and inner strength. The emotional force originates as much in what is left exposed as in the imposing musical structures surrounding it.

Their latest album, ‘The Sun Came Up Tremendously,’ has already occupied a particularly special place in my listening this year. Its reflections on memory, darkness and the persistence of light belong naturally to the poetic universe Golden Apes have been constructing throughout their career. Hearing the band live again reinforced my appreciation for their melodic intelligence, the expressive possibilities of their arrangements and their ability to make melancholy feel strangely luminous.

Golden Apes concerts have always resembled a peculiar form of meditation for me, although certainly not one deprived of movement, tension or emotional turbulence. There is a sensuous quality to their music, an invitation to inhabit its textures and subtle transformations rather than simply follow the progression of individual songs.

At Liverpool, the combination of the atmospheric lighting, the intimacy of the venue and the band’s beautifully controlled performance made the experience particularly absorbing. The Halloween setting added another dimension to their familiar musical world, but their elegance required no additional theatrical embellishment.

As the evening’s headliners, Golden Apes provided a deeply satisfying conclusion to the musical programme, one characterized by sophistication, emotional intelligence and the kind of understated intensity that has always distinguished their work.

A Celebration Worthy of Its History

The progression of the evening was particularly well conceived. Shadows Veil introduced the audience to their melodic gothic darkness and energetic post-punk sensibility; Her Own World followed with a visually striking, rhythmically forceful and beautifully theatrical performance; and Golden Apes concluded the programme with their exquisite combination of melancholy, elegance, fragility and emotional power.

The three bands approached darkness from different artistic perspectives, and that diversity gave the anniversary its musical character. Halloween provided a natural setting for their respective aesthetics, while the club’s atmospheric lighting and the festive mood created a sense of occasion without reducing the concerts to seasonal entertainment.

There was also something quietly moving about celebrating Liverpool’s birthday on the threshold between October and November, when autumn seems to surrender its remaining warmth to the approaching winter. The association with Samhain gave the night an additional poetic dimension, particularly in a venue that has witnessed so many personal and musical transformations over the past thirty years.

For me, the evening held considerable personal meaning as well. I spent wonderful moments talking with musicians, DJs, the promoter, the club’s management and staff, and people who have been attending concerts and parties at Liverpool for years. There were affectionate reunions, beautiful conversations and the comforting pleasure of being surrounded by people whose lives have intersected through music.

Those encounters deserve their own account, because Liverpool’s importance cannot be measured solely by the number of concerts it has hosted. The relationships, memories and sense of continuity it has created are equally fundamental to its identity.

But that story will come separately.

For now, I want to express my appreciation for three excellent performances and for an anniversary marked with such musical diversity, elegance and affection. Liverpool has been one of Wrocław’s meeting places for alternative culture for three decades, and this Halloween night was worthy of that history.

Happy 30th birthday, Liverpool. Thank you for the music, the beautiful memories and the countless opportunities to discover something extraordinary in the company of people who share that passion.

And thank you, Shadows Veil, Her Own World and Golden Apes, for making the passage from October into November such a memorable one.

All photos: Karolina Kratochwil.

About Golden Apes

Golden Apes is a goth rock band from Berlin, Germany, founded in 1998 by vocalist Peer Lebrecht. The band’s sound draws on darker new-wave and rock influences from the 1980s, built around Lebrecht’s voice, layered guitars and a pronounced bass presence. Golden Apes released its album “Kasbek” via Aenaos Records in 2019, followed by the EP “From the Sky” in 2023 and the group’s eleventh album, “Our Ashes at the End of the Day,” on the Icy Cold label in January 2024, issued on CD and a 400-copy limited vinyl edition. The band’s twelfth album, “The Sun Came Up Tremendously,” followed on Icy Cold Records in digital, CD and vinyl formats in September 2026 and was reviewed on Side-Line the following month. With the Halloween show at Liverpool, Golden Apes added another date to a live history that has made the band a recurring presence at European gothic and dark-music festivals.

About Her Own World

Her Own World is a gothic and dark-electronic project built around vocalist Yu and producer ad-x, based in Szczecin, Poland, and active for seven years as of 2026. The band combines programmed rhythms, guitars and theatrical stage presentation, and has built its live reputation through a steadily widening touring schedule, including a support run with Project Pitchfork. Yu and ad-x discussed the project’s development, stage discipline and visual identity in a Side-Line interview published in May 2026. At Liverpool, the band performed in new red costumes designed for the Halloween date, continuing the close relationship between Her Own World’s music and its visual presentation.

items.title: Velatine releases ‘Tonight I Am a Vampire’ single
items.summary: Velatine's Loki Lockwood takes his first lead vocal on "Tonight I Am a Vampire," out October 31, 2026 on Bandcamp.
items.fullText:
Melbourne gothic/darkwave project Velatine has released a new single, “Tonight I Am a Vampire,” out October 31, 2026 on Bandcamp. The track marks the first time Loki Lockwood, the project’s sole constant member, has sung lead vocals on a Velatine release.

For the past 12 months, vocalist Holly Purnell performed live with Velatine and appeared on four singles before leaving to pursue her own music. Lockwood, previously the project’s songwriter and producer, has now stepped up to the microphone, a shift described as necessary to keep the project’s momentum going while still writing new material.

Lockwood wrote the song around imagery drawn from Anne Rice’s vampire novels and the Théâtre des Vampires, and recorded it at the project’s home studio in Melbourne, a set of attic rooms with red-painted walls that Lockwood shares with partner “The Undertaker.” The accompanying video, which opens with a walk from the street up to that studio, was shot in the same house.

“And you never lose encounters, no matter where they lead,” runs one line from the track.

“Tonight I Am a Vampire” is available as a digital download and stream on Bandcamp, with the track also on Spotify and YouTube.

Velatine is next scheduled to perform at The Retreat Hotel in Brunswick on December 11, for the Chiron album launch, backed by two guest vocalists and a keyboard player.

About Velatine

Velatine is a gothic/darkwave duo from Melbourne, Australia, formed by Loki Lockwood and Maggie Alley in late 2021. Lockwood had previously worked as a producer with the projects The Drones and Spencer P. Jones before starting Velatine. The project released its first seven-inch single, “Comic” / “No God,” in March 2022, followed by the industrial-leaning track “Deadly Requiem” that August and a second seven-inch, “Whisper Park” / “One and Only,” in November 2022, accompanied by a video directed by Mathew T Ellery.

Velatine’s debut album, “I Won’t Be Civilised,” followed in February 2023 on Spooky Records. Regular live performance since has steered the project toward a more industrial-leaning sound, heard on the “Dead Radio EP”, released July 28, 2026. Holly Purnell joined as the project’s live and recording vocalist over the following year, appearing on four singles before departing to focus on her own music.

With “Tonight I Am a Vampire,” Lockwood takes over lead vocals for the first time, with further Velatine material already written and more live shows planned into 2027.

items.title: Palindrones share video for ‘Kryne Lamiya’
items.summary: UK duo Palindrones released a video for "Kryne Lamiya," ahead of the EP "Kryne Lamiya & The Exemplary Sadness," out 27 November 2026.
items.fullText:
London dark electronic duo Palindrones released a music video for “Kryne Lamiya”, the title track from their forthcoming EP “Kryne Lamiya & The Exemplary Sadness”, due for release across streaming platforms and for download on 27 November 2026.

The video continues a narrative Palindrones has built across recent releases, centred on a dualistic cosmic force. On “Sùil Nan Diathan,” the band’s characters received the message “The Two Become The Many Become The One,” which they carried forward as “The Brightling Star”. The “Kryne Lamiya” video depicts a confrontation between The Brightling Star and an opposing figure, Kryne Lamiya, described by the band as representing isolation, entropy and the annihilation of the self into nothingness.

About Palindrones

Palindrones is a dark electronic duo from South London made up of Karen, on vocals and synth, and Jamie, on synth, percussion, electronics and vocals. The pair describe their sound as “dreamy, Industrial Synthpop” and dark electronic music that is “both hopeful and apocalyptic at once.” The duo’s album “Chapter One: With Fearful Velocity” arrived in 2023, followed that year by the single “Samadhi”. Side-Line covered Palindrones’ “Animus” single and video in March 2025; “Animus” and “Kryne Lamiya” both later appeared on the album “Chapter Two: The Slender Blade”. Palindrones released the single “The Blood Moon” in June 2026. The duo now returns to the “Kryne Lamiya” storyline with a new video and the forthcoming EP “Kryne Lamiya & The Exemplary Sadness”, out 27 November 2026.

items.title: Sonic Panda release debut album ‘Neomelodrama’
items.summary: Sino-Spanish industrial duo Sonic Panda released its debut album "Neomelodrama" on 30 October 2026 via No Where Records, featuring Mesh and Rotersand.
items.fullText:
Sino-Spanish industrial duo Sonic Panda released its debut album “Neomelodrama” on 30 October 2026 through Barcelona label No Where Records.

“Neomelodrama” runs 14 tracks, mixing new songs, two prior singles and four remixes: “Bailes Con Beelzebub”, “Art Is Dead”, “King Cobra Redux – Zeuss Mix”, “Silence Is In Vogue” featuring Oblique, “Impossible Highs” featuring Seelenpein, “Lucky Seven”, “Invisible Boy”, “Neomelodrama”, “Wolves Among Sheep”, “Always There”, “Art Is Dead – Mesh Remix”, “Bailes Con Beelzebub – Rotersand Rework”, “Wolves Among Sheep – Frank Hurman & Carlos Bayona Remix” and “Silence Is In Vogue – Matt Pop Extended Mix”.

Sonic Panda’s Pere Ibañez wrote the music and lyrics and sings lead vocals, with Seni Ren contributing backing vocals and additional arrangements; the album was produced by Carlsed. The “King Cobra Redux” mix on the album comes from Chris “Zeuss” Harris, a producer known for his work with Rob Zombie. “Neomelodrama” is available as a digital album, a limited digipack CD edition and a limited 12-inch vinyl edition with a booklet, each via No Where Records’ Bandcamp page.

About Sonic Panda

Sonic Panda is a Sino-Spanish industrial duo signed to Barcelona label No Where Records. The project released its first single, “Foreigners”, in January 2025, followed by “King Cobra” in February 2025 and the companion “King Cobra (Remixes)” EP that September. Side-Line covered the duo’s “Invisible Boy” single in March 2026, and Sonic Panda released “Bailes Con Beelzebub” with a Rotersand rework in September 2026. Those tracks, along with “Silence Is In Vogue” and other singles, now appear on “Neomelodrama”, the duo’s debut full-length album, released 30 October 2026 through No Where Records.

items.title: Horror For Breakfast release ‘Dance’ single
items.summary: Italian duo Horror For Breakfast released the single "Dance" via Gothic World Records, a track about perception, fascination and freedom.
items.fullText:
Italian experimental electronic duo Horror For Breakfast released a new single titled “Dance” through Gothic World Records, available on streaming platforms including Spotify and on YouTube.

“Dance” is built on electronic percussion and synthesizer textures. The lyrics follow a figure who draws attention without seeking it, remaining indifferent to the expectations and judgments projected onto her, a contrast between how others perceive a person and who that person actually is.

Horror For Breakfast is signed to Gothic World Records, the label that also released the duo’s debut album “Fear Entry” on 26 September 2025, issued on CD with two bonus tracks alongside its release on digital platforms.

About Horror For Breakfast

Horror For Breakfast is a duo formed in Italy in 2023 by Lily Boggs and Lord Mortimer. Their music draws on darkwave and industrial sounds along with cinematic atmospheres, moving between tension and sensuality, darkness and emotion. The duo signed to Gothic World Records, which released their debut album “Fear Entry” on 26 September 2025 on CD, with two bonus tracks exclusive to that edition, alongside the release on major digital platforms. “Dance” is Horror For Breakfast’s first single since that album. The duo is represented by The Dark Channel PR.

items.title: Ghosts in the Graveyard release ‘Monsters for the Masses: Resurrected’
items.summary: Ghosts in the Graveyard released the reissue "Monsters for the Masses: Resurrected" on 23 October 2026 via Re:Mission Entertainment, with a new video.
items.fullText:
Ten years after its 2016 debut, Seattle deathrock act Ghosts in the Graveyard released the reissue “Monsters for the Masses: Resurrected” on 23 October 2026 through Re:Mission Entertainment. The reissue remasters and re-records the band’s 2016 debut, and the band followed it on 31 October with a video for “Old Dark House: Resurrected Version.”

The original “Monsters for the Masses” came out 21 October 2016 on A.D.S.R. Musicwerks, written by Paul Morgan with lyrics by Byron C. Miller, except “Another Night,” co-written with Shelly Miller. The 13-track “Resurrected” edition remasters and re-records the original tracklist, including “Monster Mask: Resurrected Version” and “Old Dark House: Resurrected Version,” and adds a new recording of the Afghan Whigs song “Debonair,” written by Greg Dulli. Chris Longo mastered the reissue. It is available as a digital album and as a limited CD digipak edition of 100 copies, both through Bandcamp.

The reissue’s first video, for “Monster Mask: Resurrected Version,” was directed by Byron C. Miller and contains extensive flashing lights; viewers sensitive to strobing should take note before watching. The second video, for “Old Dark House: Resurrected Version,” follows the song’s seance-themed narrative from the original album.

Byron Miller on the album’s origins

Asked about the original record, Miller tied it to his move out of his previous band: “This album means the world to me. After 8 years in God Module, this was the first music project I put together, the first time I was writing most of the lyrics, defining the aesthetic.”

About Ghosts in the Graveyard

Ghosts in the Graveyard released its debut album, “Monsters for the Masses,” on 21 October 2016 through A.D.S.R. Musicwerks. The project was formed by Byron C. Miller, following 8 years as a member of God Module, together with Paul Morgan and Shelly Miller. The debut was recorded by E.J. Bastien, mixed by Michael Wimer and mastered by Jamie King. The band describes its sound as deathrock, goth, darkwave and alternative rock, and is based in Seattle.

The band signed to Re:Mission Entertainment for its most recent studio album, “Absolute Death,” previewed by the single “In the Darkness” in September 2025, the Halloween video “Walkin’ After Midnight” that October, and the video for “Nothing Can Save You” in March 2026.

“Monsters for the Masses: Resurrected” returns the band to its 2016 debut, remastering and re-recording the original tracklist and adding a new cover of the Afghan Whigs’ “Debonair.” The reissue is out now on Bandcamp, with videos for two of its tracks, “Monster Mask: Resurrected Version” and “Old Dark House: Resurrected Version,” released in October 2026.

items.title: Deceits return with Halloween single ‘Mi Amor, Mi Vampira Pt. II’
items.summary: Los Angeles post-punk duo Deceits released the single "Mi Amor, Mi Vampira Pt. II" on 31 October 2026 via Get Better Records.
items.fullText:
Los Angeles post-punk duo Deceits released the single “Mi Amor, Mi Vampira Pt. II” on 31 October 2026 via Get Better Records. The Spanish-language track is a sequel to “Mi Amor, Mi Vampira,” which the band put out in 2023.

Kevin “Puppy” Moreno plays bass, electric guitar, synthesizer and piano on the track and produced it with Raul “Riff” Cuellar, who also mixed and engineered the vocals. Francisco Saenz plays drums. Nick Townsend handled mastering. “Mi Amor, Mi Vampira Pt. II” is out as a digital single on Bandcamp.

The single arrives as Deceits continue the “Hurt As Much As Me Tour 2026,” which runs through the end of the year and into early 2027, with confirmed dates including BLOODFLOWERS – Japan Goth & Post Punk Festival in Tokyo on 21 November, Whammy Bar in Auckland on 27 November, Space Academy in Christchurch on 28 November, Valhalla in Wellington on 29 November, The Vanguard in Newtown, New South Wales, on 4 December, and The Tote in Collingwood, Victoria, on 5 December.

About Deceits

Kevin “Puppy” Moreno and Francisco Saenz co-founded Deceits in Los Angeles in late 2021. The duo plays in Spanish and English, drawing on post-punk acts such as the Cure and Bauhaus alongside the Mexican rock band Caifanes, and Moreno has described the project’s sound as a Chicano take on post-punk built around expressive singing, rhythmic variety and the physical energy of the band’s live shows.

Deceits released “Mi Amor, Mi Vampira” as a standalone track in 2023. In 2026 the band released the single “Tren Al Sur” in July, followed by “One Day You’ll Hurt As Much As Me” in August, which Side-Line covered along with a video and a run of autumn tour dates, and “The First Day Of Fall” in September.

“Mi Amor, Mi Vampira Pt. II” continues that run of singles and ties the band’s ongoing “Hurt As Much As Me Tour 2026” to a second chapter of one of its earlier songs, released as a Halloween single on 31 October 2026.

items.title: Life In Sodom – Night/Day (Digital/CD/Vinyl Album – Nutrix)
items.summary: With “Night/Day”, the American duo Life In Sodom releases its first album of entirely new...
items.fullText:
With “Night/Day”, the American duo Life In Sodom releases its first album of entirely new material since 2013. Gerrie Brand and Daniel Heinze launched the project more than 30 years ago. On this new release, they explore an introspective world of dark, deeply human themes.

The album sounds exactly as one might expect from the band: a varied, eclectic production in which Neo-Folk, Chanson, Ballads, and a subdued form of darker Rock style converge and blend seamlessly. Some tracks invite you to drift away, while others demand your full attention, evoking smiles at times and tears at others. One moment, there is a nod to The Doors; the next, they’ll catch attention of Rome fans. The deep, expressive vocals are particularly stirring, complemented by female voices that feature primarily in the background. The bonus disc contains two tracks: danceable, club-oriented versions that lean towards Future Pop.

While Life In Sodom hasn’t always entirely convinced me in the past, this album genuinely has something to offer. (Rating:8).

Listen to “He Died Of Fright”:

About Life In Sodom

Life In Sodom is an American dark wave and gothic project founded by vocalist Gerrie Brand, releasing through the band’s own label, Nutrix Recordings. The project’s debut single, “The Stains,” appeared in 1991, followed by the albums “Phantasmagoria” (1992), “Charader” (1993), “Vampire My Love” (1995), “The Physical Being” (1997) and “Haunting” (1999).

After a multi-year gap, Life In Sodom returned with “And Then We Fall” (2007), “The New Year” (2008), “Alone” (2009), “The Hollow and Haunted House” (2011) and “The World I View” (2013-2014), building a catalog of ten albums.

The duo, now driven by Brand alongside guitarist Daniel Heinze, released the EPs “Tears Run Dry” (2020) and “Fate” (2023) on Nutrix Recordings before completing “Night/Day”, released on Nutrix in 2026.
